blocks.text: That serpents do not lack the sense of hearing is also the view of OEDMANN, Part 5, Chapter 10, p. 87. And that the rattlesnake loves music and song is expressly attested by CARVER in his Account of Travels made through North America (Voyage dans l' Amerique Septentrionale), p. 372. I shall give his own words: J' en ai vû plusieurs fois, qui paroissoient en fureur, se mettre dans une posture d' ecouter et rester immobiles avec l' apparence de plaisir, pendant tout le temps, que duroit la Musique. Niebuhr tells something similar of Egyptian serpents (Reisebeschr.
Augustine, book 2, On Genesis according to the Letter, ch. 28. And book of 65 [sic] Questions, Question 44.

By a hidden art, says Hasselquist, p. 365, the viper is tamed by the serpent-catchers in Egypt; I have seen it several times with these my own eyes, while I was living in Cairo, drawn out of a sack by them with bare hands, alive, vigorous, still furnished with its large teeth, handled, and finally killed. What the ancients reported about the Marsi and Psylli has been collected by SOUCHAY in a separate paper in the Memoires de l'acad. des Inscriptions 10, p. 431, Amsterdam ed., and by I. B. and G. R. BOEHMER in the dissertations On the power of the Psylli, the Marsi and the Ophiogenes against serpents, Leipzig 1745. Whoever wants more on the charming of serpents should consult KAEMPFER, Amoenitates exoticae, fasc. 3, obs. 9, p. 565; JOH. LUDOV. SCHULZ, Neueste Geschichte der Missions-Anstalten, fasc. 32 (Halle 1787), p. 872, or, if you cannot obtain this book, Michaelis, Biblioth. Orient. Nov. vol. 5, no. 78, p. 49; LINNAEUS, Amoenitates Academicae, fasc. 6, pp. 197, 216; Bruce, Reisen zur Entdeckung der Quellen des Nils vol. 5, p. 204 (German translation made by Volkmann), with which should be compared the remarks of I. F. Gmelin in the Appendix to Bruce's Travels edited by HASSENCAMP (Anhang zu Bruce Reisen, welcher Berichtigungen und Zusätze aus der Naturgeschichte von verschiedenen Gelehrten enthält), p. 35; BECKMANN on Aristotle, De auscultationibus mirabilibus, p. 334 ff.

Unless rather the verb לחש, to charm serpents, is a denominative from לחש, serpent, which is so called from licking, the primary meaning of the root لحس [l-ḥ-s], as NIC. GUIL. SCHROEDER sufficiently shows in his Commentary on the dress of Hebrew women, Chapter 11, §6, pp. 171-175. Cf. Michaelis, Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. p. 1440.

But that this interpretation of the verb חבר is hardly probable, since neither the word itself nor the passages of the Old Testament in which it occurs bid us think of a gathering of serpents and similar creatures, is rightly observed by DAV. MILL in his Dissertation on the חרטמים and other Magi of the Orientals (the eighth of his dissertations published together, Utrecht 1724), §9, p. 130. Mill himself, however, thinks that the magi were called חברים, binders, from חבר, he bound, because they were accustomed not only to join to themselves, to summon and bring whatever they wished, but also to constrain effectively and to bind; and so they were believed able to take away the power of harming and to bring things to obedience. He tried to prove this view at length in §§10-14, but in such a way that he uses only examples drawn from Greek and Roman antiquity, and adduces none from which it would appear that this belief in the power and efficacy of the magic art also prevailed among the ancient Hebrews. I therefore agree with CHRIST. BENED. Michaelis in his Philologemata Medica §10, p. 13, who compares the Hebrew חבר with the Arabic خَبَرَ [khabara], he knew, so that חובר properly means knowing, and then magus, charmer, just as the Chaldee מְחַבַּר and the Syriac ܝܕܘܥܐ signify a charmer. For among the Orientals, words carrying the notion of being wise and knowing have passed also to charmers, sorcerers and magi, because these are thought to know more than others. Thus from חָכַם, he was wise, [III, 168] he was wise, in Exod. VII, 11 החכמים, the wise men, are joined with המכשפים, the sorcerers, and החרטמים, the Egyptian magi; and in the very passage this chapter examines, Ps. LVIII, 6, one is called חובר חברים, charming (i.e. practising, employing) charms, and מחכם, trained in wisdom, namely in the magic arts. So the Arabic طَبّ [ṭabba] means both he excelled in knowledge and he used fascination and sorcery; and عَرّاف [ʿarrāf] means soothsayer, from the root عَرَفَ [ʿarafa], he knew. But among the Latins too the saga [wise woman, witch] was named from sagire, i.e. from knowing keenly, as CICERO expressly says, On Divination book 1, ch. 31: “Sagire is to perceive keenly; hence SAGAE for old women, because they want to know many things.” Likewise we Germans call a saga eine weise Frau, from weise, wise.
